name: UV tanning bed
lead: A UV tanning bed, also called a sunbed or solarium, is a device with lamps that emit ultraviolet (UV) radiation, mostly UVA with a small amount of UVB, to produce a cosmetic tan. Horizontal beds are the most common type; stand-up versions are called tanning booths. They are found in salons, gyms, spas and hotels and, less often, in private homes [1].

Indoor tanning became widespread in Western countries from the late 1970s after the German scientist Friedrich Wolff developed UVA-dominant beds [1]. The World Health Organization has classified UV radiation, including sunbed use, as carcinogenic to humans, and the practice has been restricted for minors, or banned, in a number of jurisdictions [1][3].

Meta-analyses of observational studies associate indoor tanning with increased risk of melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer, with higher estimated risk for people who start young [1][9][10]. Other authors discuss the limits of ecological and observational evidence and the role of overdiagnosis in rising melanoma incidence [4][5]. The wiki rates the device's outcome as a temporary tan.

paras: Tanning lamps are mostly low-pressure fluorescent tubes. A typical horizontal bed has a bench and a canopy holding long fluorescent bulbs of roughly 100 to 200 watts, so the user is surrounded by lamps when the lid is closed. Maximum session length for most low-pressure beds is 15 to 20 minutes; in the United States, maximum times are set by the manufacturer according to the time needed to produce four minimal erythema doses, an upper limit laid down by the FDA [1].

Tanning booths are vertical enclosures with more lamps and typically a maximum session of 7 to 15 minutes. Some users prefer them for hygiene reasons because the only shared surface is the floor [1]. Goggles or disposable eye protection are meant to be worn to avoid eye damage; in one 2004 study, some tanners said they sometimes skipped eye protection to avoid pale marks around the eyes [1].

Modern beds emit mostly UVA with some UVB and essentially no UVC. One review cited by Wikipedia found that the UVB output of beds was on average lower than that of summer sun at latitudes between 37 degrees south and 35 degrees north, while UVA output was on average much higher [1].

In 1890 the Danish physician Niels Finsen developed a carbon-arc lamp for treating skin disease, including lupus vulgaris, and won the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine [1]. Pale skin signified high social class in Europe and the United States until the 20th century; Coco Chanel's tan after a 1923 holiday is often cited as a turning point in tanned skin becoming fashionable [1]. Physicians also promoted a "sun cure" for many ailments, and home "sunlamps" emitting a large share of UVB, which caused burns, were sold from the 1920s [1].

Friedrich Wolff, described as the father of indoor tanning, began using UV light on athletes and developed beds emitting about 95 percent UVA and 5 percent UVB to reduce burning. He is credited with inventing the sunbed in 1975; a tanning salon opened in Berlin two years later, and his devices began selling in the United States in 1978 [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, adds details about low-pressure fluorescent lamps, electronic ballasts and later engineering changes, which have not been independently verified here [2].

UV exposure damages DNA in skin cells, including cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts. Repair enzymes fix many lesions, but unrepaired damage can lead to mutations, cell death or cancer. Skin darkening is a response to this exposure [1]. A 2001 clinical study examined whether tanning protects against cutaneous DNA damage in situ [18].

Reported reasons for indoor tanning include improving appearance, getting a pre-holiday tan, feeling good, and treating a skin condition. Improving appearance is the most commonly cited reason; tanned skin is described in the literature as signifying health, beauty and youth, and some women say they believe it makes them look thinner or covers blemishes [1]. Tanners also cite relaxation, and tanning-bed exposure is reported to raise serum beta-endorphin [1]. A 2004 controlled study found that UV exposure acted as a reinforcing stimulus in frequent indoor tanners, suggesting a physiological contribution to tanning behaviour beyond appearance motives [11]. Most indoor tanners are white women aged 16 to 25, and U.S. use has declined in recent years [1].

As a cosmetic device the bed produces a tan, which fades as pigmented skin cells are shed. Vitamin D is produced when skin is exposed to UVB; Wikipedia reports that adults who used beds weekly had higher blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations, that the tanning industry has emphasised this link, and that public health bodies say the cancer risk has to be weighed against it [1].

UV radiation from the sun or tanning devices is a recognised cause of basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma [1]. A 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis in the BMJ estimated the proportion of melanoma attributable to sunbed use [10]. As summarised by Wikipedia, a 2012 analysis found a relative risk of 1.20 for ever-use of a tanning device and 1.59 for use before age 35, and a 2014 meta-analysis found a 16 percent increase overall, 23 percent in North Americans and 35 percent for those starting before age 25 [1]. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis in Cancers examined overall and early-onset melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer in relation to indoor tanning [9]. Grokipedia gives pooled increases of about 24 percent for basal cell carcinoma and 58 percent for squamous cell carcinoma [2].

Reviews note that melanoma is the most common cancer in young adults and that higher incidence in young women may partly reflect sunbed use; a 2020 review concluded that prevention advice should include avoiding sunbeds [3]. A 2025 review of melanoma incidence and mortality trends lists tanning-bed use among the variables studied [6]. A 2020 institutional registry study compared melanoma characteristics in patients with and without a history of tanning-bed use [12].

Some researchers have raised methodological questions. An invited commentary on an Icelandic analysis, which found melanoma incidence rising a few years behind increasing sunbed prevalence, cautioned that the data were ecological and that sunbed UV emissions were poorly characterised [5]. A 2022 review reported that in Danish data melanoma incidence rose steeply while mortality did not, discussed overdiagnosis and increased sun exposure as competing explanations, and attributed a transient excess of young-age melanoma in Iceland to skin burns from sunbeds [4].

UV exposure is associated with skin ageing, wrinkles, liver spots, loss of elasticity, sunburn, photokeratitis and ocular melanoma [1]. Case reports describe sunbed lentigines and sunbed-induced pseudoporphyria [13][14]. Wikipedia reports that injuries from tanning devices lead to more than 3,000 U.S. emergency room visits a year, that beds can carry microbes including Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus aureus in a 2009 New York study, and that certain medicines cause photosensitivity that can make burning more likely [1].
Dependence on indoor tanning, sometimes called tanorexia, has been described in the psychiatric and public health literature and is associated with anxiety, eating disorders and smoking [1].

Most human evidence on tanning-bed harm is observational, from case-control and cohort studies pooled in meta-analyses [9][10]. Interventional studies have mainly addressed behaviour or medical phototherapy rather than cosmetic outcomes.

A randomised controlled trial of a web-based personalised feedback intervention for frequent indoor tanners found it acceptable and engaging and raised interest in changing tanning, but did not observe lower tanning rates among participants [8]. A Danish randomised study examined determinants of sunbed use in adolescents [15]. A nationwide survey of 3,000 people aged 14 to 45 found past-year sunless tanning product use was more common among current tanning-bed users than never-users (16.1 percent versus 5.8 percent) [7].

Therapeutic studies include a randomised comparison of conventional UVA sunbed lamps with higher-UVB lamps for psoriasis [16] and a randomised trial of UVA1 therapy in systemic lupus erythematosus [17]. These evaluate medical phototherapy and do not address cosmetic tanning.

France became the first country to ban minors from indoor tanning, in 1997, and under-18s are also barred in many other European countries. Brazil banned cosmetic use of tanning beds in 2009. Commercial tanning services were banned across Australia by 2015, while private ownership remains permitted. Many Canadian provinces prohibit under-18s, and Health Canada recommends against use of tanning equipment [1].

In the United States the FDA classifies beds as moderate-risk devices and requires a warning that they should not be used by people under 18. No federal ban applies to minors, but many states ban or restrict use by minors [1]. New Zealand relies on a voluntary code of practice, and surveys have found high non-compliance [1].

Sunless tanning products such as DHA-based tanners are discussed as an alternative that does not use UV. A survey study notes that these products are sometimes seen as a healthy alternative, but may lead people to overestimate their natural skin type and so to risky tanning behaviour [7].

lore.intro: Sunbed use is discussed on looksmax.org both as a quick way to look better and as something with serious side effects, with some members preferring natural sun. [19][20]

claims.claim: Sunbed tanning improves a man's looks, at least in the short term.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether sunbed tanning improves looks for men; one reply says it makes a person look better short term, while another says it is toxic for men and only good for women. [19]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that improving appearance is the most commonly cited reason for indoor tanning, and that tanned skin is described in the literature as signifying health, beauty and youth. [1] No study cited here compares attractiveness before and after sunbed use.

claims.claim: Going out in the sun is a better option than a sunbed.
claims.believers: A reply in a looksmax.org thread says the side effects of sunbeds are too brutal and advises just going in the sun instead. [19]
claims.experts: The World Health Organization classifies UV radiation, including sunbed use, as carcinogenic to humans, and meta-analyses associate indoor tanning with increased melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer risk, with higher estimates for those who start young. [1][9][10] Other authors discuss the limits of observational evidence and overdiagnosis in melanoma statistics. [4][5]

claims.claim: A tan is essential to looking good, so regular sunbed sessions are worth resuming.
claims.believers: A member in a looksmax.org thread says that after two years away from sunbeds he considers himself 'subhuman' without a tan and lists getting a tan as the last item on his appearance list. [20]
claims.experts: A 2004 controlled study found that UV exposure acted as a reinforcing stimulus in frequent indoor tanners, suggesting a physiological contribution beyond appearance motives. [11] Authorities cited in the article report cancer risk from indoor tanning. [1][9]
